title: Filter / Criteria Pattern
oneLiner: Builds selection logic out of small, combinable criteria objects (AND, OR, NOT) instead of one hardcoded filter function per combination.

hero.name: The Sieve
hero.catchphrase: Combine your criteria. I'll sift out exactly who matches.
hero.power: Composes reusable, combinable filter conditions to select objects matching complex, changing criteria.
hero.weakness: Break every tiny condition into its own class and a simple query can end up harder to read than the plain if-statement it replaced.
hero.origin: The Sieve appeared after a product search page grew a new hardcoded filter function for every combination requested: `filterActiveInStock()`, `filterActiveOnSaleInStock()`, `filterDiscontinuedOnSale()` — a combinatorial mess.

story.problem: The product search page has a hardcoded function for every filter combination a user might want: `filterActiveInStock()`, `filterActiveOnSaleInStock()`, and a dozen more. Every new combination means a new function.
story.solution: The Sieve introduces small, composable `Criteria` objects — `InStock`, `OnSale`, `Active` — combinable with `.and()`/`.or()`. Any combination the user picks builds itself from these reusable pieces.
story.result: New filter combinations require zero new code. Any combination of `InStock`, `OnSale`, and `Active` composes automatically from the criteria that already exist.

before: One hardcoded function per filter combination
Filter logic is duplicated across near-identical functions
after: Filter conditions are small, reusable, combinable objects
New combinations compose existing criteria — no new code
Each condition's logic is written exactly once

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A file lists a dozen near-identical filter functions, each hardcoding one specific combination of conditions.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Marketing wants 'on sale AND in stock AND not discontinued' now. That's a thirteenth hardcoded function to write.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Sieve appears holding several small mesh screens, each one a separate condition, ready to stack.
panels.speaker: The Sieve
panels.dialogue: Stop hardcoding combinations. Build small, reusable criteria instead — then combine them however you need, on demand.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: InStock, OnSale, and NotDiscontinued each implement isSatisfiedBy(product). They combine with .and().
panels.speaker: The Sieve
panels.dialogue: new InStock().and(new OnSale()).and(new NotDiscontinued()) — that thirteenth combination just composed itself from three existing pieces.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The new combination ships with zero new functions written.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Marketing's new combination composed itself from criteria that already existed. Zero new code.

useWhen: Users can combine multiple independent conditions (filters, search criteria) in ways you can't fully predict upfront.
You're accumulating a hardcoded function per filter combination, and the count keeps growing.
Conditions are naturally composable with AND/OR/NOT logic.
avoidWhen: There's only ever one or two fixed filter combinations — plain conditionals are simpler and more direct.
Breaking every condition into its own class would fragment a genuinely simple query into unnecessary ceremony.
Performance-critical filtering needs to be expressed as a single optimized database query, not composed in application code.
commonMistakes: Over-fragmenting trivial conditions into criteria classes when a single readable boolean expression would do.
Reimplementing this pattern when the underlying data store (SQL, a search engine) already provides expressive, composable query building.
Not giving criteria descriptive names, so a composed chain like `a.and(b).or(c)` becomes unreadable without knowing what each piece means.
Forgetting that composed criteria need to be evaluated efficiently — naive re-evaluation of overlapping conditions can be wasteful at scale.
explanation.realWorldExample: ORM query builders (`.where().and().or()`), search UI 'advanced filters' that let users freely combine conditions, and specification-pattern-based business rule engines are all Filter/Criteria in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just a bunch of if-statements dressed up as classes?

conversation.speaker: The Sieve
conversation.message: The individual conditions are simple, yes — the power is in COMPOSABILITY. You can combine them in ways nobody anticipated, without writing new code for every new combination.

conversation.speaker: The Sieve
conversation.message: When you're wrapping a single, permanent, never-combined condition in a whole class. If it's just `products.filter(p => p.active)` and that's all it will ever be, skip me entirely.

codeBattle.scenario: Your job-search platform lets users freely combine filters — remote-only, salary above X, posted in the last week, specific tags — in any combination, and new filter types get requested regularly.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Sieve lets each filter type be its own composable criteria object, so users can combine any subset freely without a hardcoded function for every combination.

quiz.question: What problem does Filter/Criteria solve?
options: A hardcoded function is needed for every possible combination of selection conditions
An object needs to notify listeners of changes
Two incompatible interfaces need to work together
A complex object needs to be built step by step
quiz.answer: A hardcoded function is needed for every possible combination of selection conditions
quiz.explanation: Filter/Criteria's whole purpose is letting combinations compose from small, reusable pieces instead of duplicating a function per combination.

quiz.question: How do individual criteria typically combine in this pattern?
options: Through composable and()/or()/not() operations that build a new combined criteria
By copy-pasting their logic into a new function
They cannot be combined at all
quiz.answer: Through composable and()/or()/not() operations that build a new combined criteria
quiz.explanation: Composability via logical operations is what lets new filter combinations form without new hardcoded functions.

quiz.question: When is Filter/Criteria overkill?
options: When there's only one or two fixed conditions that will never be combined
When users can freely combine many independent filter conditions
When new filter types are added regularly
When conditions are naturally composable with AND/OR logic
quiz.answer: When there's only one or two fixed conditions that will never be combined
quiz.explanation: For simple, unchanging conditions, a plain conditional is clearer than wrapping logic in composable criteria objects.

quiz.question: What's a real-world example of this pattern?
options: ORM query builders that let you chain .where().and().or() to build complex queries
quiz.answer: ORM query builders that let you chain .where().and().or() to build complex queries
quiz.explanation: Composable query builders are a widely used real-world implementation of the Filter/Criteria idea.
